Science.title: Nearly 1.7 million deaths linked to second-hand smoke in 2023, study finds
Science.summary: More than 2.7 billion people worldwide, including 767 million children, were exposed to second-hand smoke in 2023, contributing to nearly 1.7 million deaths, a Lancet study said on Tuesday. Researchers found second-hand smoke remained a major global health risk, with no safe level of exposure.

Science.summary: One day in history about 4.5 billion years ago was a dramatic one for Earth, potentially giving our planet an instant moon and an almighty headache all in one go.

Science.title: Neutrophil vesicles help Candida albicans evade immune-cell engulfment
Science.summary: The immune system is a highly sophisticated defense network designed to protect against pathogens. A research team from the Universities of Würzburg and Jena and the Leibniz Institute for Natural Product Research and Infection Biology (Leibniz-HKI) has shown that certain components of the immune system can actually help the yeast Candida albicans evade immune attack.

Science.title: Climate and air quality are closely linked, report highlights
Science.summary: An increase in pollution from wildfires and heat waves risks undermining international efforts to improve air quality and protect human and ecosystem health, according to a new report from the World Meteorological Organization (WMO), which traces the complex interrelationships between air quality and climate.

Science.summary: Researchers at the John Paul II Catholic University of Lublin (KUL) and the University of Eastern Finland have developed a new model of artificial intelligence governance inspired by the teachings of Pope Leo XIV as set out in his encyclical Magnifica Humanitas. The new model is intended to ensure that AI technologies are developed and used safely, fairly and with full respect for human rights.

Science.summary: Nature, Published online: 07 September 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-02805-w Rapid technological advances are allowing researchers to identify thousands of proteins in individual cells, revealing the hidden mechanisms underlying development and disease.

Science.title: Deep biosphere has endured mountain-building and erosion over hundreds of millions of years
Science.summary: A new study reveals that microbial life deep within Earth has persisted and repeatedly flourished through hundreds of millions of years of mountain-building and erosion. By analyzing minerals, fluids and gases from a 2.3-kilometer-deep (1.4-mile-deep) borehole in central Sweden, researchers have uncovered episodic bursts of methane-producing life linked to major geological events that shaped Scandinavia. The paper is published in the journal Communications Earth & Environment.

Science.title: New report offers lessons for preserving cultural heritage in crisis zones
Science.summary: The report, "Digital heritage preservation for vulnerable collections: Reflections on the Sudan Memory project history and inventory," was authored by Dr. Laura Gibson, senior lecturer in digital content management education at King's, alongside Sara El-Nager, independent researcher and editor, and Dr. Hannah Ishmael, lecturer in digital culture & race. It draws on 14 interviews conducted by El-Nager with contributors to the Sudan Memory project, the first mass digitization project ever undertaken in Sudan.

Science.title: A child's first 5 years set them up for life. African study explores how to target education spending
Science.summary: The first five years of life lay an important foundation for children's future schooling, health and earnings. Yet over 77% of children in sub-Saharan Africa don't have access to early childhood care and education. This places them at risk of not reaching their development potential.

Science.title: Are there nuclear weapons hidden in space? Why a 60-year ban on space nukes has been impossible to enforce
Science.summary: Nuclear weapons have been banned from space for nearly 60 years. A new detection method could help verify whether nations are keeping that promise.

Science.title: Popular brain supplement linked to shorter lifespan in men
Science.summary: A large study involving more than 270,000 people has linked higher blood levels of the amino acid tyrosine to a shorter lifespan in men. Using both observational data and genetic analysis, researchers found that elevated tyrosine could potentially reduce male life expectancy by nearly a year, while no significant effect appeared in women. Tyrosine is found naturally in protein-rich foods and is also sold as a supplement for boosting focus and mental performance, making the finding especially intriguing.

Science.title: What can a pair of underpants tell you about your vegetable garden?
Science.summary: This summer, 115 participants in Leiden and The Hague worked with scientists from Leiden University to investigate the soil life in their community garden plots. With mangetout peas, a taste test, a buried pair of underpants and a harvest festival, they helped scientists better understand the connection between soil, plants and people.

Science.title: How Indigenous Protected Areas became a vital way to protect nature in Australia
Science.summary: When you think of conservation in Australia, chances are you'll think of a national park.

Science.title: Labor Day in space: NASA astronauts get the holiday off
Science.summary: Like their compatriots here on Earth, the three NASA astronauts living aboard the International Space Station will get a well-deserved rest on Labor Day.

Science.title: Bumpy battery surfaces can masquerade as nanoscale ion pathways, misleading material design
Science.summary: A signal that appears to show ions moving inside a battery may, in fact, be an illusion caused by an uneven surface. A KAIST research team has identified the origin of this type of artifact, which can lead researchers to misinterpret what is happening inside a battery, and has developed a method to reduce it.

Science.title: Crime is falling—but the public doesn't feel safer, UK study finds
Science.summary: Crime levels are falling for most offenses across the UK—but the public doesn't necessarily feel safer. It's a human trait to focus on frightening information in the news or on social media—but it could also mean that people are more fearful about crime than they need to be.

Science.title: Port Hills research reveals 'fire trap' risk from non-native grass
Science.summary: New research from Te Whare Wānanga o Waitaha | University of Canterbury (UC) examining the aftermath of the February 2024 Port Hills wildfire found that some young native trees and shrubs were able to resprout after being badly damaged by fire.

Science.title: 'Heel-strike' may have allowed early humans to walk farther—at the cost of high-impact forces
Science.summary: The average person takes thousands of steps each day, instinctively walking heel-to-toe. Although they hardly register them, those consistent heel-first strides are more distinctive to humans than previously thought and allowed early hominins to walk farther and more efficiently, but at the cost of higher impact forces on bones and joints, according to a new study led by a researcher at Penn State.

Science.title: Stripped-down LSD reveals structural features linked to hallucinogenic and therapeutic effects
Science.summary: University of California, Davis, researchers have stripped down LSD to the base features responsible for its hallucinogenic and therapeutic effects.

Science.title: Isaac Newton’s remarkable year — and the plagiarism accusations that followed
Science.summary: Nature, Published online: 07 September 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-02808-7 A deep dive into Newton’s major work, Principia Mathematica, reveals his hate of hypotheses and a habit of courting controversy.

Science.title: The future of Earth observation: Private satellites and AI bring benefits but also pose risks
Science.summary: We've entered a new world of Earth observation, in which artificial intelligence helps researchers make sense of an ever-glowing glut of privately gathered data.

Science.title: Park rangers and residents speak up to save Togo's last national park
Science.summary: A few years ago, I drove with an old friend from Togo, West Africa, towards the country's last remaining large protected area, Fazao-Malfakassa National Park. Our destination was the Hotel Fazao, where his uncle had once worked as a professional chef after its opening in 1980. For decades, while the park was managed by the Swiss Franz Weber Foundation (FWF), the hotel had hosted tourists from around the world who came to see elephants, monkeys, and other wildlife for which Africa is famous.

Science.title: Inexpensive blue pigment enables efficient one-step conversion of carbon dioxide to methane
Science.summary: A common blue pigment could help turn carbon dioxide (CO₂) from an industrial waste product into a useful fuel. A joint research team led by Tohoku University's Advanced Institute for Materials Research (WPI-AIMR), in collaboration with Hokkaido University and startup AZUL Energy, has developed a catalyst that converts CO₂ directly into methane (CH₄) with high efficiency using copper phthalocyanine, an inexpensive and readily available blue pigment.

Science.title: Entangled particles revive a 35-year-old test of the Standard Model
Science.summary: Physicists at the BESIII Collaboration have breathed new life into a decades-old test of one of the Standard Model's most important ideas, using a technique that had gone almost untouched by experimenters for 35 years.

Science.title: War drama Pressure depicts D‑day's weather forecast—what we found when we recreated the challenge using modern systems
Science.summary: Meteorologist James Stagg gave what many regard as the most important weather forecast in history in June 1944. The fate of more than 150,000 Allied troops preparing to invade the Normandy beaches on D-Day and the future of the war in Europe depended on Stagg and his forecasting teams. Get the forecast wrong and an already perilous invasion might not succeed, prolonging the war. In the briefing room at Southwick House near Portsmouth, waiting for the forecast, sat General Dwight D. Eisenhower.

Science.title: How climate change may amplify the impact of earthquakes in the Arctic
Science.summary: Permafrost refers to permanently frozen ground. The rock is held together by ice, much like cement binds concrete. However, when the ice thaws, the ground becomes weak and unstable. During an earthquake, this can trigger a series of natural hazards. An international research team investigated precisely such an event.

Science.title: New nitride semiconductor expands material options for more powerful electronics
Science.summary: Polar wurtzite nitride semiconductors, such as aluminum nitride (AlN) and gallium nitride (GaN), are central to modern high-power and high-frequency electronic devices because of their wide band gaps, high breakdown electric fields, and strong spontaneous and piezoelectric polarization.

Science.title: Slender crystal's blue-to-yellow glow could make invisible forces visible
Science.summary: Applying pressure to luminescent organic crystals usually brings molecules closer together and weakens their fluorescence. Materials that instead brighten and undergo a large color change are rare, and clear design principles for achieving both responses in simple, rigid aromatic hydrocarbons have been lacking.

Science.title: 'The Jungle Book' offers an unconventional tool for undergraduate economics education
Science.summary: Research in the International Journal of Pluralism and Economics Education argues that "The Jungle Book" can serve as an unconventional teaching tool for undergraduate economics, using the original stories by Rudyard Kipling as well as Disney film adaptations to introduce concepts ranging from scarcity and sustainability to happiness and development.

Science.title: Reversible electric control unlocks persistent chiral phonon states
Science.summary: Atoms in a material are rarely still. They jiggle back and forth in collective lattice vibrations known as phonons. Their motion can also carry a rotational element: In 2023, scientists at PSI experimentally proved the existence of chiral phonons, which exhibit handedness depending on which way they rotate.

Science.title: Organic farming outperforms wildflower strips on profits while both improve farm biodiversity
Science.summary: What makes more sense when farming wheat—strips of wildflowers along fields or organic farming? Both options provide financial support via the European Union as environmentally friendly and sustainable farming practices. An international research team, including researchers from the University of Göttingen, has compared the ecological and economic benefits of these two farming methods in fields planted with winter wheat.

Science.title: Guldhøj folding chair: The only completely preserved chair from Bronze Age Europe
Science.summary: The remarkably preserved wooden folding chair was likely a status symbol and was found in the grave of a Bronze Age chieftain.

Science.title: Survey of young researchers raises concerns over future of science in U.S.
Science.summary: One-third of young scientists who had been planning careers in academic research changed their minds in the spring of 2025, according to a new survey. Fewer expected to remain in higher education or work in the U.S., or felt that pursuing a Ph.D. was the right decision.

Science.title: From strays to territory bosses: Epigenetics makes cheetahs adaptable
Science.summary: The findings of a new study led by the Leibniz-IZW on Namibian free-ranging cheetahs (Acinonyx jubatus jubatus) demonstrate that epigenetic mechanisms might play an important role in how animals develop different phenotypes despite their low genetic diversity. The work is published in the journal Molecular Ecology.

Science.title: Why 'you're smart' can backfire: Young children may cheat more after ability praise
Science.summary: Parents and teachers might think telling kids "they're smart" is a helpful way to build self-confidence and support positive development.

Science.title: Yes, passing 1.5 C of global warming is cause for alarm, but not despair
Science.summary: The news has been full of headlines about findings from a United Nations report: The world is set to exceed the 1.5°C global warming target set out in the 2015 Paris Agreement. The report has raised concerns and questions about what a 1.5°C increase could mean for our world.
